claims.claim: No rescue of prohemocyte differentiation phenotypes is observed by selectively restoring Cora and NrxIV in the gut in respective hypomorphic mutants.
claims.source: In comparison, in control experiments no such rescue was observed by selectively restoring Cora and NrxIV in the gut using myo1A-Gal4 (Morgan et al., 1995; Figure 2—figure supplement 1g,g', Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–d) in their respective hypomorphic mutants.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by control rescue experiments showing no effect when SJ components are restored in the gut.

claims.claim: Depleting Cora and NrxIV in neuronal tissues, fat body, gut, muscle, and salivary gland does not result in significant effects on LG hematopoiesis.
claims.source: To explore the possibility that Cora and NrxIV are involved in mediating these other modes of regulating hematopoiesis in the LG, Cora and NrxIV were also depleted in neuronal tissues (with elav-Gal4), the fat body (lsp2-Gal4) the gut (myo1A-Gal4) (Morgan et al., 1995), muscle (mef2-Gal4), and salivary gland (AB1-Gal4); no significant effects on LG hematopoiesis were observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1o–r',Figure 2—figure supplement 2e–r).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in hematopoiesis when SJ components are depleted in other tissues.

claims.claim: Over-expression of NrxIV, but not Cora, suppresses plasmatocyte differentiation.
claims.source: However, over-expression of NrxIV, but intriguingly not Cora, suppressed plasmatocyte differentiation (Figure 3d–d'',f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of Cora and NrxIV overexpression on plasmatocyte differentiation.

claims.claim: Over-expression of Cora or NrxIV in the PSC does not affect crystal cell differentiation or PSC cell numbers.
claims.source: No dramatic effects on either crystal cell differentiation or PSC cell numbers were observed (Figure 3e–e'',f' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing no significant changes in crystal cell differentiation or PSC cell numbers upon overexpression.

claims.claim: Infection with B. subtilis or E. coli results in decreased expression of SJ components in the LG, particularly in the PSC.
claims.source: We found that infection, using either feeding or systemic infection models, with either B. subtilis or E. coli resulted in decreased expression of SJ components in the LG, particularly in the PSC (Figure 4a–c'; Figure 4—figure supplement 1j–l'', m–n').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced SJ component expression upon infection.

claims.claim: Expression of SJ components in salivary gland, fat body, foregut, or hindgut is not affected upon systemic infection with E. coli.
claims.source: We also investigated if the expression of SJ components in other organs like the salivary gland, fat body, foregut or hindgut is affected upon infection and observe that there is no significant difference in the expression levels of SJ components upon systemic infection with E. coli (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a–l).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing no significant changes in SJ component expression in other organs upon infection.

claims.claim: Upon infection, the permeability barrier at the PSC is abolished.
claims.source: Importantly, upon infection the permeability barrier at the PSC was abolished (Figure 4d–f'',g,h; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c–f).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by dye permeability assay data showing loss of barrier function upon infection.

claims.claim: Infection with B. subtilis or E. coli leads to an increased number of PSC cells.
claims.source: Infection with either B. subtilis or E. coli also led to an increased number of PSC cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative cell counting data upon infection.

claims.claim: Infection with B. subtilis or E. coli results in a 4-5-fold increase in prohemocyte differentiation.
claims.source: Finally, we observed a 4–5-fold increase in prohemocyte differentiation upon infection, using either P1 (Asha et al., 2003; Kurucz et al., 2007) or Eater-dsRed as plasmatocyte markers (Tokusumi et al., 2009) and Hnt as crystal cell marker (Figure 4i–p; Figure 4—figure supplement 1o–r''; Benmimoun et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative differentiation data upon infection.

claims.claim: Over-expressing SJ components in the PSC prior to infection abrogates loss of the permeability barrier and increased differentiation of plasmatocytes or crystal cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, over-expressing SJ components in the PSC prior to infection using collier-Gal4 abrogated these outcomes; there was no loss of the permeability barrier, as well as no increased differentiation of plasmatocyte or crystal cells and no increase in overall PSC cell numbers (Figure 5a,b–e and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–h, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–i').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that overexpression of SJ components prevents infection-induced changes.

claims.claim: Knockdown of SJ components in the PSC confers a survival advantage to flies infected with B. subtilis or E. coli.
claims.source: Consistent with this, knockdown of SJ components in the PSC conferred a survival advantage to flies infected with either B. subtilis or E. coli using either a feeding or a systemic infection model (Figure 4q–r'; Figure 4—figure supplement 1s,t).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data showing improved survival upon infection in SJ knockdown flies.

claims.claim: Larval infections that disrupt the permeability barrier confer a long-term advantage that improves the ability of adult flies to survive bacterial infection.
claims.source: Moreover, larval infections, that disrupt the permeability barrier, confer a long-term advantage that improves the ability of adult flies to survive bacterial infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data showing long-term effects of larval infection on adult survival.

claims.claim: Depletion of SJ components does not induce endogenous activation of AMP reporters in uninfected controls.
claims.source: In wild-type controls AMP reporters were only detected following infection; importantly, depletion of SJ components did not induce the endogenous activation of AMP reporters in uninfected controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–l').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data showing no activation of humoral immune response in uninfected SJ knockdown flies.

claims.claim: Over-expressing SJ components in the PSC does not compromise the ability of flies to survive bacterial infection.
claims.source: Intriguingly, over-expressing SJ components in the PSC did not compromise the ability of flies to survive bacterial infection suggesting that other immune mechanisms may take over in such a scenario (Figure 5—figure supplement 2j).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data showing no negative effect of SJ overexpression on survival upon infection.

claims.claim: Depletion of SJ components in the PSC causes a significant increase in the number of plasmatocytes, crystal cells, and Ad1 positive hemocytes in early pupal stages compared to controls.
claims.source: Depletion of SJ components in the PSC caused a significant increase in the number of plasmatocytes, crystal cells, and Ad1 positive hemocytes compared to controls whereas lamellocyte counts were not affected (marked with P1 or Eater-dsRed for plasmatocytes, C5 or BcF6GFP or BcF6mcherry for crystal cells, L1 for lamellocytes and Ad1 was used for specifically labeling adult hemocytes (and not embryonic/larval ones), respectively: Figure 6a–f,g–i'; Honti et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative hemocyte counting data in early pupal stages.

claims.claim: There is a marked increase in the number of adult circulating plasmatocytes and crystal cells following SJ depletion in the PSC compared to controls.
claims.source: This effect was long-lasting as there was a marked increase in the number of adult circulating plasmatocytes and crystal cells as compared to the controls (Figure 6k–l'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative hemocyte counting data in adult flies.

claims.claim: The population of embryonically derived hemocytes remains fairly stable in cora mutants.
claims.source: This analysis showed that the population of embryonically derived hemocytes remained fairly stable (Figure 6j–j'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data distinguishing embryonic from larval hemocytes.

claims.claim: Hemocytes are activated upon larval bacterial infection as shown by initiation of filopodial extensions.
claims.source: Finally, hemocyte activation was also confirmed via another assay, the initiation of filopodial extensions, upon larval bacterial infection (Regan et al., 2013) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g–h'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by morphological data showing filopodial extensions in hemocytes upon infection, citing a previous study.

claims.claim: Toll and Relish are detected in the PSC.
claims.source: Intriguingly, Toll as well as the Imd pathway component Relish were both detected in the PSC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a–f'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing protein localization in the PSC.

claims.claim: The PSC responds to wasp infestation by activating the Toll-NFκB signalling.
claims.source: Interestingly, an earlier study has shown that the PSC responds to wasp infestation by activating the Toll-NFκB signalling (Gueguen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: Activating the Toll or Imd pathway in the PSC, systemically, or ubiquitously causes loss of the permeability barrier.
claims.source: Activating either the Toll or Imd pathway in the PSC, systemically, or ubiquitously caused loss of the permeability barrier (Figure 7a–f,j; Figure 7—figure supplement 2a–c').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by dye permeability assay data showing loss of barrier function upon pathway activation.

claims.claim: Localized activation of the Toll pathway in the PSC results in down-regulation of Coracle.
claims.source: Consistent with this, localized activation of the Toll pathway in the PSC resulted in the down-regulation of Coracle (Figure 7—figure supplement 1g–h'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced Coracle expression upon Toll pathway activation.

claims.claim: Activating the Toll and Imd pathways causes prohemocytes to differentiate into plasmatocytes and crystal cells.
claims.source: Moreover, activating the Toll and Imd pathways caused the prohemocytes to differentiate into plasmatocytes and crystal cells (Figure 7g–i'; Figure 7—figure supplement 2d–k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased differentiation markers upon pathway activation.

claims.claim: Expressing activated Toll in the larval fat body induces hemocyte differentiation in the LG.
claims.source: This data is consistent with previous results showing that expressing activated Toll in the larval fat body induces hemocyte differentiation in the LG (Schmid et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: Combining Toll and Imd pathway mutants with mutant alleles of NrxIV or cora provides substantial rescue of lethality following infection.
claims.source: Strikingly, we found that compromising the permeability barrier using mutations in SJ components was able to partially rescue dominant loss-of-function Toll and Imd pathway mutants. Typically flies heterozygous for the Toll and Imd pathway mutants spz2ca1and RelE20, respectively, die shortly after infection, but combining them with mutant alleles of NrxIV or cora provided substantial rescue of this lethality (Figure 7k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by survival assay data showing genetic interaction between SJ components and immune pathway components.

claims.claim: Neither spz2ca1 nor RelE20 mutants exhibit the characteristic down-regulation of Cora upon infection that is seen in wild-type controls.
claims.source: In further support of the idea that the Toll and Imd pathways act upstream to control permeability barrier function at the PSC, we observed that neither spz2ca1 nor RelE20 mutants exhibited the characteristic down-regulation of Cora upon infection that was seen in wild-type controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1i).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing no change in Cora expression upon infection in immune pathway mutants.

claims.claim: Inability to inactivate the permeability barrier in spz2ca1 and RelE20 mutants is accompanied by failure to induce plasmatocyte and crystal cell differentiation or induce hemocyte dispersal in 12 hr APF pupa.
claims.source: Consistent with our other observations, this inability to inactivate the permeability barrier was accompanied by failure to induce plasmatocyte and crystal cell differentiation or induce hemocyte dispersal in 12 hr APF pupa (Figure 8b,b',d,e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1a,a',c,c',g–h' and m).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing reduced differentiation and hemocyte dispersal in immune pathway mutants.

claims.claim: Double mutants for spz2ca1 with NrxIV or cora and RelE20 with NrxIV or cora show induction of plasmatocyte and crystal cell differentiation and increased hemocyte dispersal in 12 hr APF pupa both before and after bacterial infection.
claims.source: To explore in detail the genetic inter-relationship between SJs and the Toll and Imd pathways we investigated double mutants for either spz2ca1 with NrxIV or cora and RelE20 with NrxIV or cora. These double mutants showed induction of both plasmatocyte and crystal cell differentiation and increased hemocyte dispersal in 12 hr APF pupa both before and after bacterial infection (Figure 8a–a'',c–e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1b,b',d–e',f–f'' and i–m).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing restored differentiation and hemocyte dispersal in double mutants.

claims.claim: The range of BMP signals is extended further from the PSC following depletion of SJ components.
claims.source: The transgenic Dpp reporter Dad-GFP revealed that the range of BMP (Bone morphogenetic protein) signals was extended further from the PSC following depletion of SJ components (Figure 9i–k'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data showing extended BMP signaling range upon SJ depletion.

claims.claim: The levels of the Wg ligand at the PSC are reduced by depletion of SJ components in the PSC.
claims.source: Specifically, the levels of the Wg ligand at the PSC were reduced by depletion of SJ components in the PSC but increased by overexpression of SJ components in the PSC as compared to the controls (Figure 9h and Figure 9—figure supplement 1m–p'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing changes in Wg protein levels upon SJ manipulation.

claims.claim: Upon depletion of SJ components, Wg levels are lower throughout the LG, not just the PSC.
claims.source: Upon depletion of SJ components Wg levels were observed to be lower throughout the LG, and not just the PSC, consistent with the reduction in number of prohemocytes which have been shown to express Wg (Sinenko et al., 2009; Figure 9—figure supplement 1m–p'').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced Wg levels throughout the LG, citing a previous study showing Wg expression in prohemocytes.

claims.claim: The expression of dMyc is elevated following SJ knockdown in the PSC.
claims.source: Also in line with this model, we find that the expression of dMyc, which is typically downregulated by BMP signals in the PSC, is elevated following SJ knockdown in the PSC suggesting a reduced level of BMP signal (Figure 9—figure supplement 2d–f',h; Pennetier et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased dMyc expression upon SJ knockdown, citing a previous study on BMP regulation of dMyc.

claims.claim: Elevating the levels of the Wg ligand at the PSC rescues prohemocyte differentiation phenotypes caused by Cora or NrxIV knockdown.
claims.source: Intriguingly, elevating the levels of the Wg ligand at the PSC rescued prohemocyte differentiation phenotypes caused by Cora or NrxIV knockdown (Figure 9a–g and Figure 9—figure supplement 1a–l',q).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing restoration of normal differentiation upon Wg overexpression.

claims.claim: Depletion of dMyc in the PSC following knockdown of SJ components rescues the PSC cell number phenotype but does not affect plasmatocyte differentiation.
claims.source: Similarly depletion of dMyc in the PSC following knockdown of SJ components rescues their PSC cell number phenotype though it does not affect plasmatocyte differentiation (Figure 9—figure supplement 2i–l', o,m–n').
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data showing partial rescue of phenotypes upon dMyc depletion.

claims.claim: The expression of Dally like protein (Dlp) is decreased following SJ knockdown in the PSC.
claims.source: For example the expression of Dally like protein (Dlp) was decreased following SJ knockdown in the PSC (Figure 9—figure supplement 2a–c',g).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced Dlp expression upon SJ knockdown.

claims.claim: Dlp is highly expressed in the PSC where it regulates BMP signaling.
claims.source: Dlp, a heparan sulfate proteo-glycan, is highly expressed in the PSC, where it regulates BMP signaling (Pennetier et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: The observed decrease in Dlp following SJ depletion can account for some of the phenotypes such as an increase in the number of PSC cells.
claims.source: The observed decrease in Dlp following SJ depletion can account for some of the phenotypes we observe such as an increase in the number of PSC cells (Figure 2a–d, Figure 2—figure supplement 3a''–c''',g',h–j',n and Figure 2—figure supplement 4d–f',n; Pennetier et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed decrease in Dlp and its known role in regulating PSC cell numbers, citing a previous study.

claims.claim: The expression of Cora is not altered by abrogation of Wingless or BMP signaling pathways.
claims.source: Of note, the relation between SJ components and the Wingless and BMP signaling pathways is not bi-directional since the expression of Cora is not altered by abrogation of either pathway (Figure 9—figure supplement 3a–d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing no change in Cora expression upon pathway abrogation.

claims.claim: Bacterial and viral infections are known to cause breakdown of permeability barriers.
claims.source: Bacterial and viral infections are known to cause breakdown of permeability barriers (Guttman and Finlay, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: In vertebrates, activation of the immune system and interferon production are known to cause a reduction in the expression of occluding junction components and breakdown of permeability barriers.
claims.source: Indeed, in vertebrates, activation of the immune system and interferon production are also known to cause a reduction in the expression of occluding junction components and breakdown of permeability barriers (Watson et al., 2005; Edelblum and Turner, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Prominent expression of tight junction and/or the presence of a permeability barrier has been described as integral to many vertebrate stem cell niche models including adult neural stem cells, germline stem cells, and human hair follicles.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, prominent expression of tight junction and/or the presence of a permeability barrier has already been described as integral to many vertebrate stem cell niche models including the adult neural stem cells (Tavazoie et al., 2008), germline stem cells (Oatley and Brinster, 2012) and human hair follicles (Brandner et al., 2003; Meyer-Blazejewska et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The Toll and Imd pathways are induced following infection by gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, respectively.
claims.source: The Toll and Imd pathways are induced following infection by gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, respectively (De Gregorio et al., 2002; Ferrandon et al., 2007), and the EGFR pathway is induced following wasp infestation (Sinenko et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The EGFR pathway is induced following wasp infestation.
claims.source: The Toll and Imd pathways are induced following infection by gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, respectively (De Gregorio et al., 2002; Ferrandon et al., 2007), and the EGFR pathway is induced following wasp infestation (Sinenko et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: Wasp infestation is presently the only known immune challenge that affects LG function, since following infestation the PSC induces prohemocyte differentiation.
claims.source: Wasp infestation is presently the only known immune challenge that affects LG function, since following infestation the PSC induces prohemocyte differentiation (Crozatier et al., 2004; Sinenko et al., 2011; Ferguson and Martinez-Agosto, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The Toll pathway is active in the LG.
claims.source: It has been shown that the Toll pathway is active in the LG (Qiu et al., 1998; Chiu et al., 2005), specifically, the PSC responds to wasp infestation by activating the Toll-NFκB signalling (Gueguen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Stem cell-niche interactions have been shown in multiple systems to be regulated by cell junctions, such as cadherin-based adherens junctions and integrin-based Cell-ECM adhesions.
claims.source: Stem cell-niche interactions have been shown in multiple systems to be regulated by cell junctions, such as cadherin-based adherens junctions and integrin-based Cell-ECM adhesions (Tanentzapf et al., 2007; Ellis and Tanentzapf, 2010; Chen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: In the fly testes an occluding-junction based permeability barrier has a crucial role in regulating stem cell differentiation by enclosing the differentiating germline in an isolated compartment.
claims.source: For example, in the fly testes an occluding-junction based permeability barrier has a crucial role in regulating stem cell differentiation by enclosing the differentiating germline in an isolated compartment (Fairchild et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: In the fly testes, SJs block external signals from reaching the germline and thus restrict the range of niche-derived stem cell maintenance cues.
claims.source: In this system, SJs block external signals from reaching the germline and thus restrict the range of niche-derived stem cell maintenance cues. In the absence of SJs the range of niche-derived stem cell maintenance cues is greatly extended (Fairchild et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: SJ mediated regulation of the signalling microenvironment at the niche can control niche size.
claims.source: Moreover, SJ mediated regulation of the signalling microenvironment at the niche can control niche size (Fairchild et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: Occluding junctions have been implicated in the control of intestinal stem cells in Drosophila.
claims.source: Similarly, occluding junctions have been implicated in the control of intestinal stem cells in Drosophila (Resnik-Docampo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: The primary lobe of the lymph gland is organized into three regions: the PSC at the posterior end, the Medullary Zone (MZ) housing prohemocytes, and the Cortical Zone (CZ) containing differentiated hemocytes.
claims.source: The primary lobe is organized into three regions: at the posterior end is a well-defined hematopoietic niche (also known as PSC or Posterior Signalling Centre). This niche is connected to the Medullary Zone (MZ), which houses the prohemocytes, while the differentiated hemocytes are found in the Cortical Zone (CZ) (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of lymph gland anatomy and is illustrated in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: Prohemocytes can differentiate into three blood cell types: plasmatocytes, crystal cells and lamellocytes.
claims.source: Prohemocytes can differentiate into three blood cell types: plasmatocytes, crystal cells and lamellocytes (Evans et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2005), which perform the immune functions of phagocytosis, melanization, and encapsulation, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Plasmatocytes, crystal cells, and lamellocytes perform the immune functions of phagocytosis, melanization, and encapsulation, respectively.
claims.source: Prohemocytes can differentiate into three blood cell types: plasmatocytes, crystal cells and lamellocytes (Evans et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2005), which perform the immune functions of phagocytosis, melanization, and encapsulation, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of hemocyte function and citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The PSC provides a micro-environment that contributes to LG homeostasis, possibly by acting as a source for signals that are essential for regulating the production of differentiated hemocytes.
claims.source: The PSC provides a micro-environment that contributes to LG homeostasis, possibly by acting as a source for signals that are essential for regulating the production of differentiated hemocytes (Mandal et al., 2007; Krzemień et al., 2007; Pennetier et al., 2012; Benmimoun et al., 2015; Oyallon et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Multiple signalling pathways act simultaneously to regulate hematopoiesis in the lymph gland including Wingless, Hedgehog, JAK/STAT, Dpp and Notch.
claims.source: The signalling environment in the lymph gland is highly complex, with multiple pathways acting simultaneously to regulate hematopoiesis including Wingless, Hedgehog, JAK/STAT, Dpp and Notch (Lebestky et al., 2003; Krzemień et al., 2007; Mandal et al., 2007; Sinenko et al., 2009; Pennetier et al., 2012; Dey et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Mutations that perturb signalling pathways in the lymph gland result in severe disruptions to hematopoiesis including loss of the prohemocytes or hematopoietic malignancies.
claims.source: Mutations that perturb these signalling pathways result in severe disruptions to hematopoiesis including loss of the prohemocytes or hematopoietic malignancies (Crozatier and Vincent, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: The PSC is the source of cell signalling ligands including Dpp, Hedgehog and Wingless which are required for prohemocyte maintenance or for regulating blood cell differentiation.
claims.source: The PSC in the primary lobe of the LG is known to be the source of a number of cell signalling ligands including Dpp, Hedgehog and Wingless which are all required for prohemocyte maintenance or for regulating blood cell differentiation (Mandal et al., 2007; Sinenko et al., 2009; Pennetier et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Pvr, STAT and ADGF-A act outside of the PSC to regulate prohemocyte maintenance.
claims.source: Addional signalling molecules, such as Pvr, STAT and ADGF-A are known to act outside of the PSC to regulate prohemocyte maintenance (Mondal et al., 2011; Mondal et al., 2014; Khadilkar et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Increased production of differentiated hemocytes is one of the main ways by which flies could possibly respond to infection as in the case of wasp infestation.
claims.source: Increased production of differentiated hemocytes is one of the main ways by which flies could possibly respond to infection as in the case of wasp infestation (Krzemień et al., 2007; Márkus et al., 2009; Sinenko et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The humoral immune response in flies is largely based on the production of antimicrobial peptides (AMP).
claims.source: The humoral immune response is largely based on the production of antimicrobial peptides (AMP) while the cellular arm is largely mounted by the hemocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of Drosophila immunity.

claims.claim: The cellular arm of the immune response in flies is largely mounted by the hemocytes.
claims.source: The humoral immune response is largely based on the production of antimicrobial peptides (AMP) while the cellular arm is largely mounted by the hemocytes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of Drosophila immunity.

claims.claim: There are two waves of hematopoiesis in Drosophila, the first of which occurs in the embryo.
claims.source: There are two waves of hematopoiesis in Drosophila, the first of which occurs in the embryo. While embryonic hemocytes persist into later stages, a second wave of hematopoiesis takes place in a specialized organ called the Lymph Gland (LG) in larva (Evans et al., 2003; Hartenstein, 2006; Holz et al., 2003; Márkus et al., 2009; Stofanko et al., 2008; Makhijani et al., 2011; Zaidman-Rémy et al., 2012; Leitão and Sucena, 2015; Vlisidou and Wood, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: A second wave of hematopoiesis takes place in the Lymph Gland (LG) in larva.
claims.source: There are two waves of hematopoiesis in Drosophila, the first of which occurs in the embryo. While embryonic hemocytes persist into later stages, a second wave of hematopoiesis takes place in a specialized organ called the Lymph Gland (LG) in larva (Evans et al., 2003; Hartenstein, 2006; Holz et al., 2003; Márkus et al., 2009; Stofanko et al., 2008; Makhijani et al., 2011; Zaidman-Rémy et al., 2012; Leitão and Sucena, 2015; Vlisidou and Wood, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The LG consists of the primary lymph gland lobe and a series of posterior lobes (secondary lymph gland lobes).
claims.source: The LG consists of the primary lymph gland lobe and a series of posterior lobes (secondary lymph gland lobes).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of lymph gland anatomy.

claims.claim: The primary lobe serves as the main site of hematopoiesis in larvae.
claims.source: The primary lobe serves as the main site of hematopoiesis in larvae while the functional importance of the posterior lobes is currently not well defined (Jung et al., 2005; Kalamarz et al., 2012; Letourneau et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The functional importance of the posterior lobes of the lymph gland is currently not well defined.
claims.source: The primary lobe serves as the main site of hematopoiesis in larvae while the functional importance of the posterior lobes is currently not well defined (Jung et al., 2005; Kalamarz et al., 2012; Letourneau et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Prohemocytes in the posterior lobes tend to be more proliferative but express markers like DE-cadherin and JAK/STAT receptor, Domeless similar to the primary lobe prohemocytes.
claims.source: The prohemocytes in the posterior lobes tend to be more proliferative but, similar to the primary lobe prohemocytes, express markers like DE-cadherin and JAK/STAT receptor, Domeless (Jung et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: When stem cells divide the daughter cells can either self-renew to replenish the stem cell population or differentiate to give rise to a particular cell type.
claims.source: When stem cells divide the daughter cells can either self-renew to replenish the stem cell population or differentiate to give rise to a particular cell type (Fuchs and Chen, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study and represents established knowledge in stem cell biology.

claims.claim: Producing too many stem cells can result in tumor formation while producing too many differentiated cells depletes the stem cell population.
claims.source: Stem cell differentiation and self-renewal are tightly regulated as producing too many stem cells can result in tumor formation while producing too many differentiated cells depletes the stem cell population (He et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of a previous study.

claims.claim: Hematopoiesis is the production of new blood cells from hematopoietic progenitor cells, known as prohemocytes in Drosophila.
claims.source: An important biological process where stem cell-niche interactions play a key regulatory role is the process of hematopoiesis, the production of new blood cells from hematopoietic progenitor cells, known as prohemocytes in Drosophila.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of hematopoiesis.

claims.claim: Drosophila hematopoiesis produces blood cells, called hemocytes, that have specialized and essential functions in mediating fly immunity.
claims.source: Drosophila hematopoiesis produces blood cells, called hemocytes, that have specialized and essential functions in mediating fly immunity.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of Drosophila immunity.

claims.claim: Circulating hemocytes contribute to the immune response and promote survival upon oral infection.
claims.source: It is known that circulating hemocytes contribute to the immune response and promote survival upon oral infection (Braun et al., 1998; Charroux and Royet, 2009; Regan et al., 2013; Defaye et al., 2009; Nehme et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: The bacterial load of flies having PSC-specific depletion of SJ components is lower compared to control flies 24 hr post systemic infection with E. coli.
claims.source: To test this further, an in-vivo bacterial clearance assay was performed on adult flies, this assay showed that the bacterial load of flies having PSC- specific depletion of SJ components is lesser as compared to the control flies after 24 hr post systemic infection with E. coli (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in-vivo bacterial clearance assay data.

claims.claim: Hemocytes derived from adult flies bearing PSC-specific depletion of SJ components have an enhanced ability to phagocytose GFP-tagged E. coli compared to hemocytes from controls.
claims.source: Furthermore, an ex-vivo bacterial phagocytosis assay demonstrated that the hemocytes derived from adult flies bearing PSC- specific depletion of SJ components had an enhanced ability to phagocytose GFP- tagged E. coli as compared to the hemocytes from the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–d).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ex-vivo phagocytosis assay data.

claims.claim: The 40-70 kDa exclusion size observed at the PSC is consistent with the large-pore non-selective mechanism and is larger than that seen to date for epithelia in the fly, which is in the range <10 kDa.
claims.source: The 40–70 kDa exclusion size observed at the PSC is consistent with the large-pore non-selective mechanism and is larger than that seen to date for epithelia in the fly, which is in the range <10 kDa, perhaps indicating the LG SJs are highly specialized (Lamb et al., 1998; Paul et al., 2003; Genova and Fehon, 2003).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison with known permeability barrier properties in other fly tissues, citing previous studies.

claims.claim: Secreted signalling proteins known to regulate prohemocyte differentiation such as Wg and Dpp are within the 40-70 kDa exclusion size range.
claims.source: Secreted signalling proteins known to regulate prohemocyte differentiation such as Wg and Dpp, are within the 40–70 kDa exclusion size range.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the known molecular weights of Wg and Dpp and the measured exclusion size of the permeability barrier.

claims.claim: Pathogens are known to attack permeability barriers as this provides increased access to the tissues in the body.
claims.source: The breakdown of the permeability barrier in the PSC may represent an evolutionary adaptation to infection, since pathogens are known to attack such barriers as this provides increased access to the tissues in the body (Guttman et al., 2006; Guttman and Finlay, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous studies.

claims.claim: Modulation of occluding junctions may represent a general feature of stem-cell niche systems.
claims.source: As evidenced by our previous studies in the testes (Fairchild et al., 2015; Fairchild et al., 2016), modulation of occluding junctions may represent a general feature of stem-cell niche systems.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from previous studies in the testes and the current study in the lymph gland.

claims.claim: Occluding junctions play a novel and important role in shaping the stem cell microenvironment to regulate stem cell maintenance and differentiation.
claims.source: Taken together, our work suggests that occluding junctions play a novel and important role in shaping the stem cell microenvironment to regulate stem cell maintenance and differentiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data presented in the study.

results.result: Septate junctions (SJs) form a size-selective permeability barrier at the PSC in the Drosophila lymph gland. The barrier excludes molecules between 40-70 kDa, with SJ components Coracle and NeurexinIV enriched in the PSC. RNAi-mediated knockdown of these components abolishes the barrier.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C11 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches: dye permeability assays (C1-C5), protein localization by immunofluorescence (C6-C7), electron microscopy showing SJ structures (C8-C9), and loss-of-function experiments (C10-C11). The Dual Dye Assay with quantitative co-localization analysis (C5) provides robust quantitative support. The size-exclusion range is well-defined by testing multiple dextran sizes.

results.result: Loss of SJ components in the PSC leads to increased PSC cell numbers and dramatically increased prohemocyte differentiation into plasmatocytes and crystal cells (5-10 fold increase), with a corresponding decrease in prohemocyte numbers. Even partial reduction of SJ components causes increased differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C16 are supported by extensive quantitative data using multiple markers and genetic approaches. The differentiation index measurements (C14) provide quantitative rigor. The use of heterozygous mutants (C16) demonstrates dose-sensitivity. The Dome-MESO analysis (C15) confirms prohemocyte depletion accompanies differentiation, supporting a model of prohemocyte conversion rather than independent expansion of differentiated cells.

results.result: The prohemocyte differentiation phenotypes caused by SJ loss are specifically due to PSC function, as demonstrated by tissue-specific rescue experiments. Restoring SJ components in the PSC rescues the phenotype, while restoration in other tissues (gut, fat body, neurons, muscle, salivary gland) does not.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 provide strong evidence for PSC-specific function through complementary rescue and control experiments. The positive rescue in PSC (C17) combined with negative results in other tissues (C18-C19) effectively rules out systemic effects. However, the authors acknowledge that PSC drivers may have some expression outside the lymph gland, introducing minor uncertainty about absolute tissue specificity.

results.result: Overexpression of NeurexinIV, but not Coracle, in the PSC suppresses plasmatocyte differentiation, while neither affects crystal cell differentiation or PSC cell numbers.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 are supported by experimental data showing differential effects of the two SJ components. The selective effect of NrxIV on plasmatocytes but not crystal cells suggests pathway-specific regulation. However, the mechanism underlying the differential effects of Cora vs NrxIV overexpression is not explained and represents an interesting observation requiring further investigation.

results.result: Bacterial infection with B. subtilis or E. coli causes breakdown of the PSC permeability barrier through decreased expression of SJ components specifically in the lymph gland (not other organs), leading to increased PSC cell numbers and 4-5 fold increase in prohemocyte differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 demonstrate infection-induced barrier breakdown through multiple lines of evidence: reduced SJ protein expression (C22), tissue specificity (C23), functional barrier loss by dye assay (C24), and downstream cellular effects (C25-C26). The tissue-specific effect (C23) strengthens the conclusion that this is a targeted response rather than general tissue damage. The phenotypic similarity to genetic SJ loss supports a causal relationship.

results.result: Overexpression of SJ components in the PSC prevents infection-induced barrier breakdown and differentiation. Conversely, genetic knockdown of SJ components confers survival advantage upon bacterial infection, with long-lasting effects extending to adult stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 provide gain-of-function (C27) and loss-of-function (C28-C29) evidence linking barrier function to infection response. The survival advantage (C28) and long-term effects (C29) demonstrate functional significance. However, the mechanism by which increased hemocyte production improves survival is inferred rather than directly demonstrated in these claims, though it is addressed by later claims about cellular immune response.

results.result: SJ depletion in the PSC activates the cellular immune response without activating the humoral response. This results in increased circulating plasmatocytes, crystal cells, and adult hemocytes in both pupal and adult stages, with the increase primarily from lymph gland-derived (not embryonic) hemocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 distinguish cellular from humoral immunity and trace hemocyte origins. The AMP reporter data (C30) rules out humoral activation. The lineage tracing with gcm-Gal4 (C34) provides strong evidence that increased hemocytes are lymph gland-derived. The long-lasting effects (C33) demonstrate this is not a transient response. The filopodial extension assay (C35) confirms hemocyte activation, though this relies on citation of a previous study for the methodology.

results.result: Flies with PSC-specific SJ depletion show enhanced bacterial clearance, with lower bacterial loads 24 hours post-infection and enhanced phagocytic ability of hemocytes in ex vivo assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 provide mechanistic support for the survival advantage observed in C28. The in vivo bacterial clearance (C91) and ex vivo phagocytosis assays (C92) directly demonstrate improved immune function. These functional assays strengthen the conclusion that increased hemocyte numbers translate to improved immune defense.

results.result: Toll and Imd immune signaling pathways are present in the PSC and their activation (PSC-specific, systemic, or ubiquitous) causes permeability barrier breakdown and prohemocyte differentiation. Toll pathway activation in the PSC downregulates Coracle expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 establish immune pathways as upstream regulators of barrier function. The presence of pathway components in PSC (C36) is shown by immunofluorescence. The functional connection is demonstrated by multiple activation methods (C38, C40). The downregulation of Coracle (C39) provides a molecular mechanism. Citation of previous work (C37, C41) provides context, though the current study extends these findings to bacterial infection.

results.result: SJ components genetically interact with Toll and Imd pathways. Mutations in SJ components partially rescue lethality of Toll (spz2ca1) and Imd (RelE20) pathway mutants following infection. These immune pathway mutants fail to downregulate Cora upon infection and fail to induce hemocyte differentiation, but double mutants with SJ components restore differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 provide strong genetic evidence for epistatic relationships. The rescue of immune mutant lethality by SJ mutations (C42) is a striking result supporting the model that barrier breakdown is downstream of immune signaling. The failure of immune mutants to downregulate Cora (C43) and induce differentiation (C44), with restoration in double mutants (C45), provides clear genetic ordering of the pathway. This is sophisticated genetic analysis that strongly supports the proposed regulatory hierarchy.

results.result: SJ depletion alters the PSC signaling microenvironment by extending BMP signaling range and reducing Wingless (Wg) ligand levels. This leads to elevated dMyc expression and decreased Dlp expression. Overexpressing Wg rescues differentiation phenotypes, while dMyc depletion rescues PSC cell number phenotypes. The relationship is unidirectional as Wg/BMP pathway abrogation does not alter Cora expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C55 provide mechanistic insight into how barrier loss affects signaling. The Dad-GFP reporter (C46) and Wg immunostaining (C47-C48) provide direct evidence of signaling changes. The rescue experiments with Wg (C50) and dMyc (C51) demonstrate functional significance, though dMyc depletion only rescues PSC cell numbers, not differentiation, indicating pathway-specific effects. The unidirectional relationship (C55) is important for establishing SJs as upstream regulators. However, the mechanisms by which barrier loss specifically affects these pathways (concentration vs. range vs. protein stability) remain somewhat unclear.

results.result: The 40-70 kDa exclusion size at the PSC is consistent with large-pore non-selective permeability mechanisms, is larger than epithelial barriers in Drosophila (<10 kDa), and encompasses key signaling proteins like Wg and Dpp that regulate prohemocyte differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 provide important context for interpreting the barrier's function. The comparison to epithelial barriers (C93) is supported by citations and suggests specialized function. The observation that Wg and Dpp fall within the exclusion range (C94) is inferred from known molecular weights and provides a plausible mechanism for how the barrier regulates signaling. However, direct demonstration that these specific proteins are excluded would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The findings fit into broader biological contexts: infection-induced barrier breakdown is known in other systems, occluding junctions regulate multiple vertebrate stem cell niches, and similar mechanisms operate in other Drosophila stem cell systems (testes, intestine). This suggests occluding junction modulation may be a general feature of stem cell niche regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C67 and C95-C97 place the findings in broader context through citations of previous work. These contextual claims are well-supported by the literature cited. However, C96 and C97 are more speculative, representing interpretations and generalizations from the current and previous work rather than direct experimental findings. The speculation is reasonable given the evidence but represents a hypothesis for future testing rather than a demonstrated result.

results.result: Background information on Drosophila hematopoiesis and lymph gland organization: the lymph gland contains a PSC niche that regulates prohemocytes through multiple signaling pathways (Wg, Hh, JAK/STAT, Dpp, Notch), prohemocytes differentiate into three hemocyte types with immune functions, and there are two waves of hematopoiesis (embryonic and larval).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C90 provide essential background information, all supported by citations to previous literature or established knowledge. These claims establish the biological context necessary for interpreting the novel findings. While not novel results from this study, they are accurately represented and appropriately cited.

results.result: Background on Drosophila immune pathways: Toll and Imd pathways are induced by gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria respectively, EGFR pathway is induced by wasp infestation, and the Toll pathway is active in the lymph gland with the PSC responding to wasp infestation.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 provide background on immune signaling, all supported by citations. These establish the known immune responses in Drosophila and set up the novelty of the current findings regarding bacterial infection effects on the lymph gland. The claim that wasp infestation was the only known immune challenge affecting LG function (C61) provides important context for the significance of the bacterial infection findings.
